Most Warlords are recent. The war produced them — people whose talent for command revealed itself under conditions that made talent impossible to hide, who found themselves directing dozens and then hundreds and then more because the alternative was losing. Five years later they occupy an awkward position in a world that no longer needs them in the same way. Some have transitioned into political roles in the Abyssal Lands, their military authority translating imperfectly into civilian governance. Others have found that the skills transfer well to the power vacuums the cold war keeps creating. The best of them are trying to build something. The rest are trying to stay relevant.

The Valis Confederacy produces a specific type of fighter that could not have emerged anywhere else — lightly armored, aggressively mobile, as comfortable fighting on a rolling deck as on solid ground, and possessed of a charisma that functions as both social currency and tactical asset. The Swashbuckler's style is performative in the best sense, every fight an opportunity to be remembered, every victory ideally achieved with enough flair that the story improves in the retelling. This aesthetic serves practical purposes in a Confederacy where reputation is a form of power and the crews that follow you do so partly because of who you are.

The blade as hobby and the blade as livelihood produce very different fighters, and both call themselves Fencers. Wealthy practitioners treat it as an accomplishment to be displayed at social occasions, their technique elegant and their actual combat experience minimal. Poorer Fencers fight in demonstration matches, private disputes, and arrangements that exist in the grey area between sport and violence, their technique equally elegant and considerably more tested. The two groups share a vocabulary and very little else, and each tends to regard the other with a contempt they consider well-earned.

Dynasia's feudal aristocracy produces Lancers as naturally as it produces everything else that requires expensive horses and years of dedicated training. They are mounted soldiers first, devastating with the spear from horseback, but the Dynasian tradition insists on competence on foot as well — particularly training against other cavalry, a specialization that proved its worth repeatedly during the war. Lancers carry the specific pride of people who have mastered something genuinely difficult and expensive, which is to say they can be insufferable at dinner but are extremely useful in a fight.

Nobody founded the Dreadnaught tradition. It emerged independently, repeatedly, across the hard places of the Abyssal Lands — the discovery that enough armor, enough will, and enough refusal to acknowledge damage can make a person functionally unstoppable in the short term. Dreadnaughts are typically the most heavily armored fighters anyone has ever encountered, and they share a psychological profile that is either admirable or alarming depending on one's perspective — an absolute unwillingness to go down that has been refined through survival into something approaching a fighting philosophy.

The Zafeer brought this tradition into Dynasia along with the Vizier, and like the Vizier it found institutional accommodation in its new home. Originally a spiritual practice — the whirling combat style a form of moving meditation, the fighter seeking union with something divine through the perfect expression of movement — it has shed most of that theological context since the Zafeer's conversion to the faith of Alister High. What remains is the technique, preserved with impressive fidelity by practitioners who have largely forgotten what it was originally for. Something in the movement still feels like prayer, even to those who would not use that word.

The Trader States have always understood that individual heroism is a liability in a supply line and a formation is only as strong as its least disciplined member. The Phalanx tradition reflects that institutional philosophy — shield walls, coordinated advances, tactics designed around the unit rather than the individual. Dynasia employs similar formations, arriving at the same conclusions through a feudal military tradition rather than a mercantile one. Phalanx fighters are uncomfortable fighting alone. They are also uncomfortable watching anyone else fight without proper formation discipline, which makes them difficult companions.

Dueling schools exist across all three Concord nations, built on the explicit premise that the sword is an equalizer — that a farmer's son with enough talent and discipline can stand across from a merchant prince's heir and have the better of it. The premise is not entirely false. The schools do produce genuine meritocracy within their walls, and the traditions they teach favor skill over strength. Outside their walls, the question of who can afford tuition quietly reasserts itself. The ideal survives contact with the world imperfectly, as ideals tend to.

The arenas of the Abyssal Lands predate the Abyssal occupation and survived it, which says something about human nature that most people prefer not to examine. They exist in grand purpose-built structures in the major cities and in basement rooms that smell of blood and coin in equal measure, and the fighters who populate them range from willing professionals chasing fame and purses to the enslaved and indentured who have no choice in the matter. Daracha Rowe was the former — a willing participant who became famous enough to have a manager, and human enough to eventually want something different. The arena did not take her retirement gracefully.

Focused martial artist who channels inner stillness into ranged precision. Gains and spends focus through movement and form transitions, using it to fuel accurate and critical ranged attacks, counter incoming fire, and support allies — with chakra position and ammunition running as parallel systems that reward switching between them.

Guardian who turns the act of protection into overwhelming offensive pressure. Challenges a single target to lock its attention, guards an ally to generate retaliatory opportunities, and combines blocking, reflection, and justice procs into a feedback loop where every defensive action arms a harder counterattack.

Reality-warping damage dealer who makes enemies doubt what they perceive. Stacks illusory damage across multiple sources and elements, then exploits it through possession, distraction, and vulnerability — with a capstone that converts all her damage output to illusory, turning every ability into a tool for the same overwhelming condition.

Divine caster who pairs a holy companion with cross-shaped area attacks that hit row and column simultaneously. Manages companion health and divinity as twin resources, using alignment charges to enhance damage or fuel healing, while cross abilities let him reshape battlefield coverage with a single action.

Patient curse-weaver who layers earth and dark debuffs onto enemies before punishing them for acting. The Forbid suite turns enemy strengths into self-inflicted wounds — counters, criticals, dodges, and heals all become liabilities — and the capstone extends every Forbid effect to the entire enemy formation at reduced chance.

Evasive illusionist who maintains a stock of mirror images as both a defensive buffer and an offensive resource. Single-target attacks have a chance to consume an image rather than land, while images can also be spent for flanks, hexes, and damage bursts — with spirit resources sustaining auras that heal allies and punish enemies through illusory retaliation.

Relentless melee aggressor who builds stacking aggravation on every hit, simultaneously raising damage and eroding her own accuracy. Expertise rewards the misses that aggravation causes, rage fuels aggravating abilities that spike both resources at once, and the capstone makes every attack inherently aggravating — letting stance and ability tags stack multiple charges on a single strike.

Deliberate long-range predator who uses hidden and aim as a preparation engine for devastating single strikes. Builds resources through patience — staying hidden, avoiding attacks, following criticals — then spends them on penetrating, phasing, or advantage-consuming shots, with a capstone that doubles reload time in exchange for proportionally amplified damage on every attack.
Centered Flow — Whenever the Drifter gains focus while already focused, he generates mana and is quickened.
Resolute Example — Whenever the Exemplar blocks an attack, his next attack before his next turn gains the justice modifier.
All is Illusion — All damage the Illusionist deals is converted to illusory damage, with increased illusory power and extended illusory duration. Does not affect damage afflictions.
All Are Forbidden — Whenever the Lore Keeper activates a Forbid ability, its effect applies to all enemies at a reduced trigger chance, in addition to the primary target at full chance.
Generate Mirror Image — The related actions have a chance to generate a mirror image on proc.
Aggravating — All attacks of the Reaver gain aggravating, reducing accuracy and increasing damage with each successive hit, resetting on miss.
Sniper Reload — Reload time is doubled, but ranged attacks deal additional damage equal to a percentage of the reload time value.
Cross Targeting — A meta-skill that modifies the targeting of other abilities, changing their targeting pattern to a cross formation.

A reactive brawler who weaponizes low health. He opens chakras by absorbing hits while endangered, converting punishment into counters, clobbering responses, and defensive tools that grow stronger the closer he is to death.

A ranged duelist who combines sustained target lock with arcane and elemental shot enhancements. She weaves pinpoint accuracy, illusory damage, and blessed strikes into her ranged attacks, generates mana through prepared vows, and stacks arrow upgrades that all fire simultaneously on a single shot at full attunement.

A fire-and-corruption specialist who channels demonic power through a companion. He builds corruption on enemies to consume for burst damage and life drain, uses malediction as a persistent marker, and corrupts or possesses the companion to weaponize it directly.

A precision attrition caster who keeps enemies alive on purpose. He locks targets at near-death through deathless abilities and spirit-sustained afflictions, extracts value from that liminal state through harrowing payoffs and possession, and requires his own dangerous condition to execute the kit's most powerful tools.

A guarded ranged specialist who protects a single ally while building power through patience. His readied abilities set him inactive while prepared, activating on the target's turn or death with effect scaled to wait time, and his ammo system lets him tailor damage type to the situation.

A studied predator who learns from the flow of combat itself. Study accumulates through hits landed and received, scaling his critical strikes, poisons, and defenses passively throughout a fight, while expertise funds hidden access and advantage powers his most devastating finishing blows.

A dual-element caster who unlocks elemental duets by using both required elements before firing. She blends elemental attunement with song-based support, disrupts and distracts through sonic abilities, and rewards elemental variety with access to paired attacks that exploit both offensive and defensive elemental mismatches simultaneously.

A psychic healer who reads the battlefield through timer and illusion. Vision abilities deliver different effects based on whether a unit's timer is high or low, influence funds healing and control, and divinity sustains a disruption-protecting domain while powering light-and-illusory offense that blends support with attrition.
Arcane Quiver — Arrow upgrade abilities do not replace one another. All currently loaded arrow upgrades apply simultaneously to the next ranged attack.

Duets — Duet abilities require the Songmage to have used both of their required elements since her last Duet. Using a Duet resets the requirement. Duets use the greater of the two associated elemental powers and target the worse of the two associated elemental defenses.
Visions — Vision abilities have two effects determined by the target's timer position. A high timer triggers one effect; a low timer triggers the other.
Specific Time — The ranges for vision abilities are reduced, but these abilities have greater effects.

Conflux Consumers
Priming Runes

A self-inflicted bleed specialist who turns his own blood into fuel. He opens wounds on himself to power bloodlust-enhanced strikes, drains life and generates anguish and spirit power from his own suffering, and carries a permanent unkillable bleed that amplifies every ability that depends on bleeding.

A smiting duelist who trades resource generation for raw power on a family of prepared strikes. Her smites sacrifice mana gain while prepared in exchange for healing, purging, shielding, or damaging effects layered onto melee attacks, while challenge and counter tools let her control and punish a single locked-on enemy.

A mana-attrition striker who punishes magical investment as readily as physical resistance. He drains, denies, and inverts enemy mana through melee, leans on form thresholds to gate his most dangerous tools, and weaves affliction and timing runes into a kit built around starving casters dry.

A standard-bearing battlefield anchor who protects allies through banners rather than personal toughness. Raising and dropping standards grants ongoing team buffs with bonus payoffs on the drop, while mounted strikes, enchantment sharing, and audience-building songs round out a support kit built around calculated vulnerability.

A precision marksman who marks enemies for death and waits for the perfect shot. He afflicts targets with hex and malediction, builds toward critical hits that trigger prepared castigations, and can layer two such judgments at once to unleash devastating dual payoffs on a single perfect strike.

A possession specialist who layers bonus effects onto her core abilities based on how much of her turn remains unspent. Discipline abilities reward holding actions in reserve, traps and possession redirect danger back onto enemies, and Teknixian ammunition lets her tailor her tools to whatever the fight demands.

An arcane pickpocket who profits from every spell she steals or disrupts. She drains mana and enchantments from enemies, converts disrupted spells directly into damage, and slips into hiding whenever her interference succeeds, turning magical theft into both her offense and her escape.

A companion-bonded fighter who grows stronger in lockstep with her summoned ally. Buffs, enhancements, and combat momentum flow freely between Synergist and companion, attacks chain off one another's successes, and the bond runs deep enough that benefits granted to either one have a chance to spill over to both.

r.t: — the foundational relationship between the Knight and a single chosen ally. Every subclass introduces its own guard variant (Full, Punishment, Purge, Delay, Maneuver, Elemental, Parry, Vengeance, Purity, Heal), but the core act of choosing someone to protect never goes away. It's the one mechanic exclusive to the Knight and the thread every subclass is required to pull on.

The Spellsword establishes a focused relationship with one enemy at a time, compelling its attention so she can protect every other ally from it while the rest of the field is free to be handled differently. Re-establishing a challenge after the first costs escalating mana, with a parallel time-cost release valve, so switching targets is a meaningful decision rather than a free action. This makes her best suited to anchoring against boss-level threats while still being able to disengage deliberately when the fight demands it.
Challenge Attacks and their Three Modes -

Every Challenge ability resolves differently depending on the situation — an Initial Effect fires only on the first use against a freshly chosen target, delivering either a powerful punish or a defining setup that shapes the relationship going forward. A Basic Effect triggers when she attacks any other enemy, letting her clear minions while still landing a rider against her challenge to maintain pressure on the boss. The Challenge Effect triggers when she attacks the challenged enemy directly, delivering the ability's most elevated payoff and rewarding her for staying locked onto the fight that matters most.

Nemesis abilities are reactive moves that trigger automatically after the challenge takes its turn, letting the Spellsword answer the boss's action without spending her own turn to do so. Each subclass's Nemesis reflects its specific identity — stunning lightning, draining flame, slowing frost, fortifying earth, redirecting shadow — turning the challenge's own aggression into the trigger for her counter-pressure. They reinforce the endurance half of her kit, giving her something to do between her own turns during a long fight against a dangerous foe.

Culmination abilities are prepared effects that pay out the moment the Spellsword's challenge dies, rewarding her for seeing the fight through to its conclusion rather than punishing her for the loss of her primary target. Each subclass culminates differently — health, mana, action, strength, or life — reflecting what that subclass values most in the moment victory is achieved. Because these abilities require an active challenge to trigger, they create a quiet incentive to land the killing blow on the challenge itself rather than letting another ally finish it.

Imbuements are ongoing preparation abilities the Spellsword grants to herself or an ally, each providing a passive proc that triggers on future attacks without needing to be reapplied. Only one imbuement can be active on any given character, and only one character can hold a given imbuement at a time, forcing real allocation decisions across a long fight. Because imbuements reserve a portion of her maximum mana for as long as they're active, every imbuement granted is also a quiet bet against her own ability to afford an expensive re-challenge later.

— the broad family of abilities where the Knight inserts himself between an ally and harm, and the specific Intercession effect where he takes the next attack outright. This pillar is what gives the base capstone its reach and what Bodyguard develops most deeply, but it shows up everywhere — Cavalier's Ride to the Rescue, Hospitaler's Stunning Intercession, Dragoon's Arcane Intercession, Crusader's Purity Guard.

— the damage-triggered resource that rewards the Knight for taking hits rather than just avoiding them. It's not gated to the Knight alone, but it's deeply woven into his identity since he's the class most likely to be standing in the way of attacks in the first place. Pain Threshold, Threshold Blow, Threshold Ire, Threshold Flurry — it surfaces in nearly every subclass as a payoff for endurance.

— the Knight's mobility and charge-attack gate. Cavalier and Dragoon lean hardest into this, but mount summons and mounted abilities appear across the spread (Champion's Accelerating Charge, Crusader's Mounted Battalion, Blackguard's Black Lance), giving the class an aggressive, mobile option that contrasts with its otherwise stationary, protective image.

— the prepared two-action ability type where the Knight and his guarded ally act in concert. It's the clearest mechanical expression of the Knight's whole purpose: he doesn't fight alone, and his strongest moments are when his guarded ally fights beside him rather than behind him.

— the ongoing resource that fuels active auras, conditions, and sustained effects. It regenerates over time and is the thing nearly every Spirit-tagged ability either spends from or drains continuously, making it the Reaper's most constant pressure point.

— the lump-sum activation cost gained on any unit's death. Distinct from Spirit Power's steady drip, Orbs gate the Reaper's biggest commitments — resurrection, the Spirit Shot family, Burial Cave-In, Premature Burial — turning death on the battlefield into permission to do something powerful.

— the overspend gauge that punishes recklessness with knockout risk but rewards it with speed, locked abilities, and enhanced effects. It's the one mechanic exclusive to the Reaper and the thread that subclasses like the Hangman and Gaslighter pull on most deeply.

— the pattern of reading an affliction's current value and cashing it out through a second ability. The Buccaneer's bleed-countdown-hex chain is the clearest expression, but Gushing Blood, Culmination of Sins, Culmination of Torments, and Whispering Maladies all share the same setup-then-payoff shape.

— the recurring pattern of abilities that simply cannot be used unless the battlefield meets a specific shape: alone, lowest health, buried, tired, intangible, possessed. Verdict, Last Rites, and Reckoning are built almost entirely from this, and it surfaces as a narrowing cost on power throughout the rest of the family.

The summon-consumes-all-ammo model: a companion's power and active duration scale with how much ammo was poured in, the ammo type locks until the companion expires or dies, and summoning a replacement frees the old lock immediately. Every subclass touches this differently — Tinker's toggled modifications, Engineer's ammo-insensitive Shield Guardian as the exception, Siege Engineer's operate-to-accelerate loop — but the underlying summon contract is identical across all of them.

The queue-and-trigger system: abilities place a detonation, riders accumulate as more get added to the same target or chain, and Detonate (or its variants — Precise Detonation, Trigger Shot, Impulse Detonation) fires the queue. This pillar is what lets a Bomber stack countdowns, a Savant accumulate concoctions, or a Reliquarian chain Shielding Detonation off a planned ammo load. It's the slowest-building but highest-payoff pillar in the family.

The prepared, snapshot-based multi-use resource: ammo is locked in at preparation time, the belt becomes undisruptable in that state, and each subsequent use draws from the snapshot rather than current ammo. This is the pillar that lets a Teknixian front-load a decision and then execute it repeatedly without re-committing resources turn to turn.

The cross-cutting pattern we just reinforced on Grenade, Teknos Shot, Timebomb, and Amplifying Shot: shared, non-subclass-specific abilities don't just change damage type per ammo, they change behavior — Air triggers a storm proc, Light doubles the hit, Dark raises the culling threshold, Mana scales off current mana, and so on. This is what makes ammo choice feel meaningful even on the most generic attacks in the kit, and it's the connective tissue that makes all twelve ammo types feel like real strategic choices rather than skins on the same number.

The foundational resource. Only one of twelve ammo types is active at a time, switching costs an action via Load abilities, and each type carries its own capacity, speed, and identity (Air's storm tag, Light's double-fire, Dark's culling threshold, Flechette's variable consumption, and so on). Every other pillar is downstream of this one — it's the dial that gets turned to make the rest of the kit behave differently.

A damage striker who tracks a living benchmark of her own striking power. Her consistency value rises and falls with deliberate choices throughout a fight, gating powerful payoffs at its peak and fueling cheaper alternatives at its floor, while form-locked fists and divine fortune round out a kit built on mastering that rhythm.

A ranged performer who keeps deadly objects in the air between shots. Building up a juggle count grants retaliation as it grows, with some attacks tapping it for value without spending it and others cashing it all in for a single devastating discharge, all while a growing audience adds further support and control.

A volatile demolitionist who turns elemental unpredictability into a weapon. Splash attacks spread lesser damage to anything standing nearby and redirect entirely if they miss, while chaotic ammunition and accumulating spirit power feed increasingly random and increasingly powerful elemental chaos.

A blade-and-spell duelist who finds her rhythm in switching between them. Striking with steel after casting and casting after striking builds escalating power, with fire as her dominant element and water as its counterweight, all anchored by a challenge she pursues with both weapon and magic alike.

A self-effacing companion fighter who steps into shadow so someone else can shine. Possession, flanking, and illusory damage round out her offense, but her defining trait is willingly weakening herself to empower her companion or an ally, growing more spectral the deeper that sacrifice goes.

A magic-devouring berserker who turns enemy spellcraft into raw sustenance. He drains mana, disrupts enchantments, and converts elemental punishment into personal fuel, growing more resistant and more replenished the more magic is thrown his way, with anguish and Wrath sharpening the hunger further.

A momentum fighter who commits fully once she starts swinging. Activating a drive locks her into a single devastating attack repeated automatically turn after turn, trading flexibility for speed and counter potential, while expertise and influence shape which flavor of relentless aggression suits the fight.

A battlefield protector who layers overlapping auras of protection and punishment. Her wards grant the team retaliation, healing, and elemental punishment simultaneously, and sustaining one refreshes them all, letting a well-managed Warder keep an entire defensive ecosystem running indefinitely.

A sustained-cast specialist who turns interruption into opportunity. Her abilities build power the longer they channel, but many deliver a distinct consolation payoff if cut short, and every disrupted channel feeds her mana regardless of which specific effect triggers.

A self-corrupting destroyer who feeds her own suffering into devastating magic. She inflicts corruption on enemies while cultivating it within herself, gating her strongest spells behind how much darkness she's willing to absorb, and converts her growing affliction directly into the substance of her attacks.

A reality-twisting manipulator who inverts fortune itself. She afflicts enemies with chaos and timed traps while flipping conditions on their heads — turning shields to curses, blessings to afflictions, luck to misfortune — bending the battlefield's fate in whichever direction serves her best.

A phase-stepping striker who exists between solid and intangible. Slipping into intangibility unlocks devastating all-in attacks that consume her entire turn, while a parallel form-based rhythm pulls her toward and away from center, rewarding total commitment to the space between worlds.

A mounted vanguard who fights as a unit with his steed. He and his mount share momentum, backbiting, and risk in equal measure, striking together, suffering together, and punishing enemies who dare to flank a mounted assault.

A trap-and-poison specialist who plants lingering damage and waits for the right moment to detonate it. Hexes sit dormant on enemies until triggered, ammunition shapes which poison or hex she deploys, and a single well-timed activation can cascade into a chain of overlapping afflictions all firing at once.

A self-sacrificing battlefield medic who channels pain into power. He bleeds enemies and bleeds himself in equal measure, trading his own health for ally buffs, and ensures that every wound he inflicts on himself ripples outward to strengthen the whole team.

A battlefield controller who decides exactly who fights whom. He marks enemies to attack specific targets, draws their aggression onto himself, and punishes every forced engagement with guaranteed counters, turning the chaos of combat into a battle fought entirely on his terms.

The other branch of that same root tradition, shaped instead toward explosive, overwhelming offense — speed and force concentrated into single decisive moments rather than Stonefist's patient endurance. Like Stonefist, Thunderfist's distinct identity emerged gradually from simple distance rather than philosophical intention, but generations of practitioners have since built a genuine and proud tradition around what started as an accident of geography.

One branch of the original unarmed tradition, grown over generations into a school defined by endurance and immovability. Stonefist practitioners train toward the unbreakable stance — absorbing punishment, refusing to yield ground, outlasting opponents rather than overwhelming them. The geography that separated them from their Thunderfist cousins centuries ago has long since calcified into a real philosophical identity, even though neither school can point to a founding disagreement that caused the original split.

Outside every formal school, lineage, and institution, certain practitioners reach a level of mastery that no longer resembles discipline at all. The Drunken Master's technique looks unsteady, almost comedic, until the moment it isn't — a flow between forms so complete that intention and improvisation become indistinguishable. They emerge from any tradition and belong to none, having gone far enough beyond their original training that the question of where they started stops being relevant.

The highest religious order among Dynasian Monks, Ascetics have taken the church's incorporation of martial training to its furthest devotional extreme — years of discipline aimed not just at combat mastery but at perfecting the body as an act of faith, drawing the practitioner closer to the divine image of the GodKing himself. Where the Crusader spreads the faith and the Templar embodies it, the Ascetic refines themselves in its image, one form and one breath at a time.

Dynasia recognized early that a tradition built on unarmed discipline, careful movement, and patient observation produces excellent spies almost by accident. Talented Monks are recruited from various schools and redirected toward espionage, serving noble houses and church interests that need discreet operatives more than they need visible warriors. Infiltrators tend to maintain whatever surface tradition trained them while quietly serving a very different purpose underneath.

What began as organized sport in the Trader States — matches, wagers, local champions — gained a harder edge during the war, when gyms that once trained athletes found themselves training soldiers instead. The sporting tradition never disappeared, but it now coexists with a more martial strain born from wartime necessity, and the two influences are visible in how differently individual Pugilists carry themselves depending on which gym shaped them.

Among the old Valisian crews, certain fighters integrated unarmed combat technique directly into raiding culture, finding it suited the chaos of close-quarters shipboard fighting where a dropped weapon could mean death. A handful of crews specialize in the method and train it formally. More often, Skirmishers are independent specialists who drift between crews, valued for a skill set that doesn't require carrying anything that can be lost overboard.

No school within the tradition sits in starker contradiction to its founder than Viper Fang. Where Vajra traces back to a man destroyed by poison, Viper Fang has built an entire practice around it — and their justification is not philosophical reclamation but practical advantage. Poisoners and assassins find Viper Fang training useful precisely because it provides camouflage: a respected martial tradition's legitimacy, worn as cover for work that has nothing to do with serenity or honor. Other schools know this, and most keep careful distance.

Named for the founder himself, the Vajra school claims direct descent from the original knight who swore off weapons after being tricked into killing his emperor's son. True to that origin, Vajra practice centers on reaction rather than initiation — countering, redirecting, answering violence rather than seeking it. It is considered the most orthodox lineage, the closest living link to a man whose entire philosophy was built from being wronged rather than from choosing to strike first.

Every practitioner of the martial tradition begins here, regardless of which school or method they will eventually pursue. The Initiate learns the foundational forms passed down since the first knight refused his blade — stances, breathing, the basic flow of chakras that the entire tradition builds upon. What an Initiate becomes depends entirely on where they train and who teaches them, which makes this the most universal and least defined stage of the path.

The most literal expression of the Knight's defining purpose, the Bodyguard exists to stand between a single charge and harm, full stop. Some serve nobility, some serve merchants wealthy enough to fear for their lives, and a smaller number serve people who have nothing to offer but need protecting anyway. The role is unglamorous compared to other Knight traditions — no banners, no temples, no tournaments — but Bodyguards take a particular pride in the purity of the function. There is nothing complicated about what they do. They simply do not let their charge die.

Watchfulness over a place rather than a person defines the Sentinel tradition. They guard gates, bridges, storehouses, shrines, and city walls with equal diligence, and the role carries no particular mystical weight — a Sentinel posted at a temple and one posted at a granary approach their duty identically. What matters is the place, and the people who depend on it remaining secure. Sentinels develop an intimate, almost territorial relationship with what they protect, and dislike few things more than being reassigned somewhere new.

Not everyone can fight their own battles, and the Champion exists to fight them instead. The role spans an unusually wide social range — Champions represent downtrodden petitioners who have no standing to demand justice themselves, and they represent nobles in formal duels and tournament tilts where personal combat would be beneath their dignity or simply unwise. The common thread is representation rather than personal stake. A good Champion fights as hard for a farmer's land dispute as for a baron's honor, which is either admirable consistency or a troubling lack of judgment, depending on who is asking.

Unlike the Templar, fully bound to the GodKing's faith, the Hospitaler maintains only a loose connection to Dynasia's church. They operate as knights without fixed borders, taking commissions and causes wherever they find them, sometimes with church sponsorship and sometimes entirely independent of it. This flexibility makes them useful in the Abyssal Lands, where Dynasian institutional authority is thin and a knight who doesn't need official sanction to act can move faster than one who does.

Mounted combat meets magical practice in the Dragoon tradition, a step beyond the purely martial Lancer. Dragoons maintain the deep bond with their mount that defines Knight culture broadly, but layer onto it abilities oriented around reflection and elemental resistance — a defensive magical sensibility that suits a tradition built around protecting others. They are less common than Lancers, requiring both the expensive cavalry training and a magical aptitude that not every aspiring mounted knight possesses.

Every virtue the Knight represents, the Blackguard inverts without abandoning the underlying structure. They still guard. They still serve a charge and take vengeance for harm done to that charge. The difference is who they choose to protect — tyrants, witches, anyone whose power justifies the investment of a Blackguard's considerable skill. They consider themselves proudly fallen rather than corrupted, having concluded that protection should flow toward power rather than need. Every Blackguard secretly aspires to invert the relationship entirely and become the one served rather than the one serving, which makes them dangerously unreliable allies even to those they currently protect.

Dynasia's aristocracy produces the Cavalier as its most stylish mounted tradition, combining the expense and prestige of cavalry training with a personal code of conduct that Cavaliers discuss at every opportunity and violate only with great personal anguish. They are proud, sometimes insufferably so, but the pride is generally backed by genuine competence and genuine commitment to the code they have adopted. A Cavalier without honor is, in their own estimation, simply a man on a horse.

The Crusader tradition reaches deep into Dynasian history, and not all of that history is comfortable to discuss. For centuries, Crusaders spread the GodKing's faith at the point of a sword, converting through conquest as much as conviction. The current GodKing's notable kindness and tolerance has redirected the tradition toward gentler purposes, and most active Crusaders today understand their role as defense of the faithful rather than expansion of the faith by force. The older mandate has not entirely disappeared, and the gap between what Crusaders once did and what they do now is a source of quiet generational tension within the order.

Dual blades and exceptional parrying define the Paragon's combat style, and the skill required to master it produces a tradition with a healthy and largely earned sense of its own excellence. Paragons carry themselves with confidence bordering on ego, but it tends to be the kind of confidence that survives contact with a real fight, which buys considerable tolerance from people who might otherwise resent it. They are selectively recruited for tasks that genuinely merit their particular talents, and they have little patience for being asked to do anything less.

The pinnacle of the Knight's devotional purpose, the Templar does not merely serve the GodKing's faith — their presence creates something like sacred ground wherever they stand, a living extension of Alister High's temple carried into the world. Where the Crusader's history is complicated and the Hospitaler's commitment is loose, the Templar's investment in the faith is total and uncomplicated by ambiguity. They represent what the Knight class aspires toward at its most complete: protection in service of something larger than the person being protected.

A relentless fighter who turns his own exhaustion into a weapon. He pushes himself past fatigue to unlock devastating self-fueled combos while punishing tired and exhausted enemies in turn, and grows nearly unstoppable the more worn down he becomes.

A trap-laying gambler who weaponizes a single shared deck of cards. She plants ranks of trapped cards across the battlefield, lets fate decide when they trigger through a slowly depleting draw, and bends song and rune magic around the chaos of the deal.

A possession-channeling conduit who turns her own body into a relay for everyone around her. Sustained channels spill their effects onto allies and enemies alike, her companion drains and reflects the push and pull of alignment, and starting any channel sends a ripple of speed through her whole team.

A dread-weaving terror who turns fear into a weapon of attrition. She floods the battlefield with mounting dread, forces enemies to freeze in place rather than act, and finishes off anyone who's already paralyzed by their own panic.

An underdog marksman who fights hardest when the odds are against him. His justice grows the stronger his target is compared to himself, rewarding every shot taken from a position of disadvantage, and peaks precisely when he's on the verge of defeat.

An opportunistic scavenger who profits from stripping power away from everyone around her. She rips buffs from her own allies to fuel devastating payoffs, commits fully to berserk fury for her most dangerous shots, and capitalizes on every act of theft with a sharper eye for the kill.

A pursuit-driven assassin who never lets a target out of his sight. He strikes from hiding against whoever last acted, tracks both friend and foe through the flow of battle, and grows deadlier the longer he stays locked onto the same prey.

A righteous purifier who turns corruption itself into ammunition. She punishes the tainted with escalating light magic, spends her divinity freely between healing and destruction, and finds a rhythm where every cure sharpens her next strike and every strike deepens her next cure.
