The clearest expression of what the Formless Ones once sought, the Telepath reaches mind to mind, reading and communicating in ways no spoken language can match. It is the most recognizable face of Psychic ability to ordinary people, and also the most uncomfortable one — nobody enjoys knowing their thoughts aren't entirely private. Telepaths who can control the depth of their reach are rare. Most simply learn to live with knowing more than anyone wants them to.

Where the Telepath reaches into other minds, the Kinetic reaches into the physical world directly, moving objects and bodies through will alone. It is the most visibly inhuman of the Psychic disciplines — there is no mistaking a Kinetic's ability for ordinary cleverness or charisma, and that visibility tends to draw exactly the kind of fearful attention most Psychics try to avoid. Among the Wagon Folk, Kinetics are valued and unremarkable. Almost everywhere else, they are watched.

Knowing things before they happen is the Diviner's gift, an extension of the Formless inheritance toward prediction rather than perception or force. Diviners read the immediate future of conflict with unsettling accuracy — what an enemy will do, how badly they're hurt, where the danger is about to come from. It is a quieter ability than Kinetic's, but no less unsettling to those on the receiving end of a stranger who seems to know exactly what's about to happen to them.

The Haunted reach toward spirits, and spirits reach back. This is among the more dangerous expressions of Psychic ability, since contact runs in both directions — a Haunted practitioner who spends years calling on the dead for insight finds the dead increasingly willing to call on them in return. The affliction is not separate from the gift. It is the gift, working exactly as it always has, simply turned around.

Making others forget is a quietly devastating ability, and the Amnesiac pays for it in kind — gaps in their own memory growing wider the more they use their gift on others. Some Amnesiacs barely remember their own childhoods. Few discuss what that cost feels like, partly because the words for it tend to slip away along with everything else.

Illusion and false perception are the Mindbleeder's tools, bending what others see and experience until reality and fabrication blur. The cost runs the same direction as the gift — Mindbleeders increasingly struggle to trust their own perceptions, uncertain where the illusions they craft for others end and their own grip on what's real begins.

Subtler than the Kinetic and quieter than the Telepath, the Hypnotist works through sustained channeling and careful, patient influence rather than dramatic displays of power. Where other Psychics force their way into a situation, the Hypnotist prefers the slow approach — suggestion building on suggestion until the target's own choices start working in the Hypnotist's favor. It is the most insidious discipline precisely because it rarely looks like anything is happening at all.

Not every Psychic's instability comes from the gift corroding them. The Mastermind's affliction runs the other way — an egotism so total that it predates and shapes how they use their ability, every act of influence bent toward proving their own brilliance. Masterminds are controlled, calculating, and genuinely effective. They are also, almost without exception, exhausting to work with.

Where the Mastermind's flaw is ego, the Puppet Master's is something colder — a manipulative streak that borders on sociopathy, expressed through literal control over others rather than mere influence. The ability and the personality reinforce each other so thoroughly that it becomes difficult to say which came first. Puppet Masters impose control because something in them needs to, and the gift simply gave them the means.

True time travel does not exist in this world, but the Chronomancer comes closer to touching time than any other discipline — manipulating its perception, and sometimes its actual passage, though only ever in a single forward direction. They can quicken a moment or stretch it thin, but never reverse it, never branch it, never escape the line everyone else is also walking. It is a profound gift with a humbling limitation built directly into its nature.

The line between Valisian pirate crews and the island folk they raid is blurrier than either side likes to admit, and the Buccaneer tradition exists in that blur. Spirit worship runs deep in both communities, mixed freely with the faith of the Trinity in a way Dynasia would find scandalous and Valis finds unremarkable. Buccaneer Reapers serve aboard ships and in island settlements alike, calling on spirits of drowned sailors and lost crews, the dead who never quite made it home being among the most pervasive and powerful presences the sea produces.

Nobles understand that fear is a useful tool, and the Executioner's public function has always been as much about the watching crowd as the condemned. Trained and retained by noble houses to perform sanctioned killings with theatrical weight, Executioners carry an uncomfortable relationship with the spirits their work generates — the newly dead rarely depart peacefully when their death was staged for someone else's political benefit.

Where the Executioner serves noble intimidation, the Hangman serves something closer to civic order, a tradition with deep roots in Dynasian frontier history. Bringing structured justice to lawless edges of settled territory, the Hangman's grim profession represents the line between chaos and a functioning community — someone has to do this so that everyone else doesn't have to resort to it themselves. The work is unloved. The function is, in its own bleak way, foundational.

The most literal relationship with death in the Reaper tradition, the Gravedigger spends their working life in cemeteries and burial grounds, and over years in that company they develop an unusually practical familiarity with spirits. Graveyards accumulate the confused and newly formed — presences that have not yet settled into understanding what they are or what happened to them. The Gravedigger's role is often simply to be present for that confusion, a familiar face in an unfamiliar transition.

Drawing on old folk tradition, the Sin Eater takes on the burdens of both the dead and the living, a function that manifests as much in purification as in consumption. Disenchanting what should not have been earned, purging what should not be carried, the Sin Eater's work toward spirits serves a similar purpose — sometimes guiding a tormented presence toward peace, sometimes recognizing that peace isn't possible and ending the spirit instead. Neither outcome is treated as a failure. Both are considered mercy, depending on what the spirit actually needs.

The four moons of the world move in patterns that Harbingers have studied for generations, reading omens in their phases and alignments the way an Astrologer reads the stars. Death, disaster, and significant turning points all seem to leave traces in that lunar pattern if a Harbinger knows how to look, and their reputation as bringers of bad news follows them everywhere. Nobody is happy to see a Harbinger arrive. Everyone wants to know what they've seen.

Dreams carry real power in this world, and the Sandman works in the space where powerful dreams cross over into spirit formation — distinct from the nightmares that spawn goblins, a darker and more chaotic phenomenon entirely. The Sandman's tradition shares an uneasy proximity with the faith of Shaetavar the Sleeping God, both concerned with what dreams can create and mean, though Sandmen generally avoid claiming any direct theological connection to a god who might, after all, still be dreaming them into being.

Communication runs in two directions for the Whisperer — listening to spirits, and using spirits to relay messages and information to others. It is an effective and unsettling skill, and the constant presence of voices that aren't quite there tends to leave a mark. Whisperers develop a particular paranoid edge over time, an inability to fully trust silence, having spent too long aware of how much can be listening that nobody else can perceive.

Death and mercy are not opposites in this tradition, and the Mercy Bringer moves fluidly between them. Sometimes mercy means ensuring a kill is quick and clean rather than prolonged. Sometimes mercy means the kill itself, ending suffering that has no other resolution. The Mercy Bringer carries the weight of being trusted with that judgment, and the best of them never stop finding it heavy.

The most quietly dangerous Reaper tradition, the Gaslighter manipulates — the living, through careful deception, and the spirits themselves, bent toward serving the Gaslighter's interests rather than their own nature or peace. It is a deliberate exploitation of the exact vulnerability that shaped Stephen Blackwell's introduction to the tradition: a spirit that looks and feels like comfort, that a grieving person desperately wants to believe, twisted by someone willing to use that desperation rather than gently correct it.

The Bandit works close to civilization rather than far from it, preying on the visitors and travelers who move through a town's outskirts while maintaining hideouts among the peasantry who either sympathize, fear them, or both. It is a profession that requires social intelligence as much as physical capability — the Bandit who cannot read a community, who cannot tell which farmers will shelter them and which will report them, does not last long in the trade.

Cities produce the Cutthroat the way they produce everything else — through density, desperation, and the particular anonymity of urban life where a body in an alley might not be found until morning. The Cutthroat is not uniquely murderous among Rogues so much as uniquely unsentimental about it, treating violence as a practical tool in the pursuit of robbery rather than a last resort. They work in cities because cities are where the money is, and because cities are where violence disappears fastest into the noise.

The ideal Burglar job ends with the victim discovering days later that something is missing. No confrontation, no witnesses, no moment where the Burglar has to make a decision about what happens if someone wakes up. They are specialists in absence — of themselves, of evidence, of any sign that the space they entered was ever touched. The craft requires patience and preparation that most other Rogues find excessive. Burglars consider it basic professionalism.

Where the Burglar avoids all contact, the Thief simply prefers not to be caught. Picking a pocket in a crowded market, lifting a purse at a festival, walking out of a shop with something that wasn't paid for — these require confidence and presence rather than technical breaking-and-entering skill. The Thief's relationship with risk is more casual than the Burglar's careful planning allows for, which produces faster work and occasionally faster consequences.

Roads are where money moves, and the Brigand knows this better than anyone. Operating in organized groups along trade routes and caravan paths, Brigands function more like an informal tax on commerce than simple robbery — predictable enough in their habits that experienced merchants factor them into shipping costs. In the Abyssal Lands, where Concord authority thins to nothing along the major routes, Brigand groups have become powerful enough to function as de facto territorial powers in their own right.

Two distinct traditions operate under the same name. The professional Assassin is a contractor — trained, discreet, available to any nation, guild, or private party with sufficient coin and legitimate enough grievance to make the risk worthwhile. The Cult of Glasya represents something more structured and more theologically invested, the most renowned killers in the known world who happen to serve a demon lord and happen to be available for hire. Engaging the Cult is not joining their faith. It is simply the most reliable way to ensure a specific person stops being alive.

The Wagon Folk produce Acrobats as naturally as they produce Mountebanks and Psychics — performance is part of their cultural identity, and physical mastery of one's own body is respected regardless of what it's used for. The criminal reputation that follows Acrobats is largely borrowed from the general suspicion that follows Wagon Folk everywhere, rather than earned by the Acrobats themselves. This does not make it less persistent or less unfair.

The Trader States built their guild system to regulate commerce, and where regulation exists, someone will find profit in circumventing it. Smugglers began as tax-evaders and traffickers of contraband, and that version still thrives in the cities and ports. The more complicated version emerged in the Abyssal Lands, where the same skills applied to moving goods the system refuses to provide to people who genuinely need them. Bryan Lowe understands both versions intimately. Which one he considers his real work probably depends on the day.

Information is currency in a cold war, and the Skulk has no institutional loyalty that would complicate turning it into coin. They specialize in stealth as a means of gathering what others don't want known — secrets, correspondences, the private conversations of powerful people — and in turning that knowledge into personal advantage through blackmail and coercion as readily as through sale. Where the Spy performs a function, the Skulk accumulates leverage.

Strip away the cultural trappings the term carries in the wider world and what remains is a practitioner who has achieved mastery of a specific and demanding craft: moving unseen, killing cleanly, extracting information without leaving evidence, using poison as a tool rather than a weapon of last resort. The Ninja tradition is less a cultural identity than a professional standard — a ceiling that the best in the broader Rogue tradition aspire toward, achieved through discipline that most of their peers mistake for something more exotic than it actually is.

The most defensively oriented of the Runemage traditions, the Abjurer specializes in protective circles and warding inscriptions, most commonly etched into armor rather than cast through the air. The tradition traces back to the earliest practical applications of Titan runic knowledge — the first thing any civilization wants from magic, once they have access to it, is to stop being hurt. Abjurers are not glamorous practitioners, but they are consistently employed.

Where most Runemages inscribe their work on objects or places, the Symbolist inscribes directly on people — runes triggered by specific actions, lying dormant until the conditions of their activation are met. The work requires both technical precision and a careful read of how a person moves and fights, since a rune that triggers at the wrong moment is either useless or dangerous. Symbolists tend to develop an unusually intimate understanding of whoever they're working with, which not everyone finds comfortable.

Among the oldest Runemage traditions, the Cabalist draws on pre-church texts that predate Harold Hugh and the founding of Dynasia's faith, pursuing the creation of golem companions through runic inscription as a form of devotional practice. The current church accommodates this tradition uneasily — those foundational texts are still used, but the old religion never imagined its god becoming flesh, and the Cabalist's work of creating artificial life sits in a theological space nobody has cleanly resolved. The golems, for their part, do not appear to have opinions on the matter.

Every major Runemage academy produces a handful of students who take their foundational training and then disappear — into remote locations, private obsessions, decades of solitary refinement. The Hermit is not self-taught, but they have long since outgrown whatever institution shaped them, pursuing runic mastery in directions no curriculum anticipated. They accumulate knowledge the way their chosen locations accumulate dust, and share it with roughly the same enthusiasm.

Born from the practical need to counter hostile magic, the Disenchanter tradition developed a philosophy as much as a technique — that another practitioner's enchantments are not just obstacles to be removed but resources to be claimed. Disenchanters fuel their own work with what they strip from others, a parasitic elegance that more orthodox Runemages find philosophically distasteful and practically undeniable.

The Scrivener's work is architectural rather than personal — runes etched into doorframes, floors, walls, and roads, waiting for the right trigger to activate. It is a patient tradition that rewards preparation over improvisation, and Scriveners tend to be most effective in environments they have had time to prepare thoroughly. A Scrivener who has spent a week in a building before a conflict begins is a significantly more dangerous practitioner than one who arrives at the same time as the enemy.

The closest any Runemage tradition comes to Wizard territory, the Sage specializes in elemental runes with an academic enthusiasm that occasionally outpaces their judgment about what the knowledge should be used for. They are among the most broadly educated of Runemage practitioners, drawn to understanding for its own sake, which produces both impressive versatility and a certain moral flexibility that more focused traditions tend to find concerning.

Weapon inscription is as old as the Titan tradition itself — the original fusion of forging and magic that gave non-magical races their first foothold against progenitor power. The Glyphic has made that ancient practice into a specialization, mastering the enhancement of weapon-etched runes beyond what most practitioners consider achievable. They carry forward the most direct lineage to the Titans' original purpose, even if most Glyphics think of themselves in considerably more practical terms.

Timing runes that last only briefly but can be consumed for dramatically amplified effect represent a particular school of runic philosophy — that power concentrated and released in a single moment outweighs power distributed across time. Cryptics are specialists in that concentrated burst, managing runes that are simultaneously fragile and explosive, requiring both precise timing and a tolerance for the risk of something going wrong at exactly the worst moment.

The pinnacle of Runemage practice, the Sorcerer has mastered power runes and, more importantly, mastered sequence — understanding not just what individual runes do but how their combination and ordering shapes reality at a fundamental level. Where other Runemages write words, the Sorcerer writes sentences, and understands the difference between a list of powerful things and a story that changes how things are. Adair Taggart, curmudgeonly and underestimated and in possession of knowledge about Hellstones that his academic peers consider beneath their attention, understands something about runic sequence that most Sorcerers spend their careers approaching.

A companion-commanding warlord who fights best at the head of an army. He buffs his companions and guarded ally simultaneously through a family of Boon abilities, coordinates joint attacks across the whole party, and finds an opening to strike whenever any companion does.

A self-afflicting fire striker who weaponizes her own suffering. She burns enemies with fire and hex, blinds herself deliberately to unlock more powerful strikes, and hits hardest when spreading a condition she's already inflicted on herself.

A self-sacrificing healer who converts his own damage into ally benefits. He absorbs punishment through backbiting, transfers afflictions from allies to himself, and pushes past death itself to heal, purge, and shield the team — with every act of self-destruction rippling outward as a gift.

A masterless warrior who fights without loyalty to anyone. He damages allies deliberately, sacrifices them for power, fights hardest when alone or outnumbered, and then atones for the destruction he causes — raising the fallen, healing the wounded, and giving back a fraction of what he took.

A melee duelist who builds momentum by staying locked onto the same target. Consecutive attacks against the same enemy stack Tempo, layering debuffs and powering up her offensive and elemental tools, with a deliberate reset rewarding a burst of speed before she picks a new target to hunt.

A precision caster-archer who chains ranged and magic attacks off each other's critical hits. She builds aim and mana as parallel resources, alternates between elemental ranged and spell attacks to trigger Follow Up chains, and scores a free attack of the opposite type whenever either side crits.

A poison-and-influence specialist who layers multiple damage conditions simultaneously. She applies poisons through melee, magic, and hex, scales their effects with influence built from illusory damage, and converts her entire magic toolkit into a poison delivery system with her capstone.

A battlefield engineer who turns the field itself into a weapon. She layers switches, fuses, and rune-based traps simultaneously, arms and enhances them all at once, and creates chain reactions where one triggered trap cascades into the next.
Follow Up Remedy – Following purging affliction from self with purging same affliction from ally (Acolyte)

Luck Domain – Afflicts all enemies with unlucky accuracy each turn. Requires a minimum divinity to activate and drains divinity each turn. Generates divinity when enemies miss due to unlucky accuracy. (Acolyte)
Luck Prayer – Grants an ally lucky based on devotion. Mana cost is also dependent on devotion (Acolyte)
Lucky Heal – Gain lucky healing for next heal this turn (Acolyte)
Lucky Magic – Gain lucky damage for next magic attack this turn (Acolyte)
Passing Purge – Low power purge without preparation (Acolyte)
Purging Regeneration – Disenchant target ally of regeneration to purge. Purge power is based on regeneration remaining. (Acolyte)
Second Treatment – Follows failing to purge with purging again (Acolyte)
Basic Regeneration – Grants a single ally regeneration (Acolyte)
Fortune’s Benediction – Heals ally with blessed and heal enhanced by divinity. Grants the healed lucky for a period based on overheal. Spends one divinity. (Acolyte)
Fortune’s Cure – Prepared heal with blessed. (Acolyte)
Regeneration Benediction – Heals ally with heal enhanced by divinity; grants regeneration based on overheal. Spends one divinity. (Acolyte)
Sacred Vulnerability – Afflict target with light vulnerability (Acolyte)
Speed Benediction – Heals ally with heal enhanced by divinity; quickens ally based on overheal. Spends one divinity. (Acolyte)
Divine Hex – Afflicts a single target with a light-based hex consuming all divinity for increased effect. (Acolyte)
Fortune’s Brilliance – Magic light attack versus all with blessed (Acolyte)
Fortune’s Light – Magic light attack versus single with blessed (Acolyte)
Global Regeneration – Grants all allies regeneration (Acolyte)
Hex Deliverance – Afflicts enemy with long duration, high potency, low damage light hex (Acolyte)
Medical Strike – Melee attack following purge enhanced by potency of affliction purged (Acolyte)
Overwhelming Light Benediction – Heals ally with heal enhanced by divinity; possesses ally and grants light add to attack based on overheal. Spends one divinity. (Acolyte)
Sacred Shine – Light magic attack that enhances next heal based on damage (Acolyte)
True Fortune – Prepared spell. Heals all allies and grants them lucky damage and lucky accuracy (Acolyte)
Unlucky Hex – Light hex and unlucky accuracy versus target (Acolyte)
Vessel Benediction – Heals ally with heal enhanced by divinity; deals light damage to all enemies based on overheal. Spends one divinity. (Acolyte)
Defense Addendum – Single target heal that enhances defense based on amount healed (Healer)
Infusion of Divinity – Next heal is enhanced by divinity (Healer)
Life Domain – Grants all allies regeneration each turn. Requires a minimum divinity to activate and drains divinity each turn. Generates divinity when any ally overheals. (Healer)
Power from Preservation – Enhance damage of next attack based on healing done this turn (Healer)
Supper Prayer – Increases healing received by allies. At high levels grants healing spells a chance to stay prepared (Healer)
Ameliorative Heal – Single target heal that ameliorates damage afflictions (Healer)
Assault Heal – Heal ally and quicken and enhance damage overheal (Healer)
Damage Purge – Purges damage afflictions from a single target (Healer)
Death Ward, Greater – Targets all allies, no allies can be affected by death effects until the healer’s next turn (Healer)
Enlightening Heal – Single target heal that restores target mana based on overheal (Healer)
Purging Addendum – Single target heal that purges target based on amount healed (Healer)
Quick Heal 1 – Single target heal that does not require preparation (Healer)
Radiant Addendum – Single target heal that grants target light damage add based on amount healed (Healer)
Deny Death – If one target ally would die before the Healer’s next turn, that ally survives at one health until its own turn, dying at the end of that turn if not healed. (Healer)
Divine Retaliation – Deals light damage to a single enemy and grants self and all allies light retaliation based on divinity. Consumes all divinity (Healer)
Group Heal, Greater – Level 2 Heal on all allies (Healer)
Heal, Greater – Level 2 Heal on one ally (Healer)
Healing Blow – Melee attack that heals ally with lowest life (Healer)
Holy Cleansing – Purges multiple afflictions from one target. Number of afflictions removed scales with divinity spent. (Healer)
Luminous Addendum – Heals all allies and deals light damage to target based on amount healed (Healer)
Luminous Hex – Afflicts target enemy with light hex. Consumes 3 divinity (Healer)
Restoration Blast – Untyped magic attack versus all that deals damage based on healing done this turn (Healer)
Restoration Bolt – Untyped magic attack versus single that deals damage based on healing done this turn (Healer)
Rise to Battle – Raise ally who makes basic attack (Healer)
Ultimate Heal – Consume all mana to heal all allies a massive amount based on mana spent. (Healer)
Ameliorative Strike – Melee attack that ameliorates all damage afflictions on party (Disciple)
Corruption Retribution – Corrupt damage to single target based on corruption purged since last turn (Disciple)
Divine Beam – Light magic attack against column that lowers elemental power and elemental resistance, consumes all divinity (Disciple)
Elemental Retribution – Follows purging an elemental affliction. Deals elemental damage to all enemies for each elemental affliction purged (Disciple)
Elemental Spread – Follows purging an elemental affliction. Afflicts all enemies with the purged elemental affliction (Disciple)
Immaculate Blow – Melee attack that enhances affliction resist of disciple and lowers affliction potency of all present afflictions (Disciple)
Purging Preparation Blow – Melee attack that enhances purge power until end of turn (Disciple)
Purging Wave – Purges afflictions from all allies (Disciple)
Sacred Light Beam – Light magic attack versus column. Consumes up to 5 divinity (Disciple)
Sanctuary of Innocence – Prevents any ally from being affected by an affliction until next turn. Generates divinity on preparation. (Disciple)
Affliction Ward – Enhances affliction resistance of single target and generates divinity (Disciple)
Annul Corruption – Converts the next corruption against target to regular damage (Disciple)
Elemental Barrier – Enhance all elemental resistances of team (Disciple)
Elemental Lucidity – Purge team of all elemental afflictions (Disciple)
Immaculate Totality – Purge corrupt damage from all enemies and allies (Disciple)
Physical Purge – Purge physical afflictions from a single target (Disciple)
Physical Redoubt – Enhances physical resistance of entire team, generates divinity (Disciple)
Physical Ward – Enhances physical resistance of a single target, generates divinity (Disciple)
Air Purge – Purges air element afflictions from a single target and enhances air resistance (Disciple)
Earth Purge – Purges earth element afflictions from a single target and enhances earth resistance (Disciple)
Fire Purge – Purges fire element afflictions from a single target and enhances fire resistance (Disciple)
Physical Bastion – Single target physical resistance enhancement, reserves mana and can only be used on one ally at a time (Disciple)

Protection Domain – Protection Domain: Increases affliction resistance for all allies each turn. Requires a minimum divinity to activate and drains divinity each turn. Generates divinity when any ally successfully resists an affliction. (Disciple)
Restoration Prayer – Increases purge power. At high levels, grants purges a chance to stay prepared. (Disciple)
Water Purge – Purges water element afflictions from a single target and enhances water resistance (Disciple)

A divine trickster who turns healing against those who use it. She disrupts and cancels enemy heals, punishes accumulated healing with retroactive damage, and wraps genuine support tools in a kit designed to make recovery itself a liability.

A form-shifting melee performer who builds power through sequential dance steps. Each dance ability advances a shared step counter that escalates in effect, the Flourish abilities unlock after the first step, and staying in the right form amplifies her speed and accuracy while she moves.

A frightened-target specialist who converts fear into precision payoffs. She builds fear across the battlefield, drains life and aim from frightened enemies, and grows deadlier the more thoroughly she's already terrified her targets.

A rift-summoning technomancer who fights alongside elemental companions. She summons fire, frost, and lightning rifts as specialized combat partners, coordinates detonations and ammo to empower them, and quickens her companion every time a detonation resolves.

A melee psychic who unravels enemies from within. She builds influence through combat, afflicts targets with insanity to trigger unpredictable behaviors, and layers possession and illusory damage on top of a challenge relationship that lets her press the most vulnerable mental points.

A mana-hungry berserker who treats her spell reserves as both a weapon and a fuel source. She scales her magic and melee damage with total mana, converts backbiting damage back into mana through her capstone, and commits fully to berserk for her most powerful spells.

A proc-driven melee fighter who coats her weapon in a persistent elemental effect. She cycles through six Glamors to change her attack proc, shares that proc with allies, amplifies rune and critical procs through stances, and ensures that every proc that misses makes the next one more likely.

A disruption-resistant protector who turns being interrupted into a weapon. She guards an ally behind malediction and hex walls, uses Mordant abilities to punish anything that tries to disrupt her preparations, and counters any enemy effect that fires against her with an attack of her own.
Celestial Bolt – Single target light magic attack with piercing that procs additional light damage on critical (Priest)
Celestial Brilliance – Light magic attack with piercing against all that procs additional light damage on critical (Priest)
Celestial Storm – Randomly targeting light magic attack with four attacks and piercing that procs additional light damage on critical (Priest)
Celestial Strike – Single target light melee attack with piercing that procs additional light damage on critical (Priest)
Divine Blessing – Grant all allies damage shield and light retaliation based on damage shield. Retaliation is lost with damage shield. Consumes all divinity (Priest)
Guarding Bolt – Single target light magic attack that grants Priest damage shield based on damage (Priest)
Guarding Storm – Magic light storm attack that grants Priest damage shield based on total damage (Priest)
Lattice Bind – Light magic damage and delay based on Priest’s damage shield. Consumes damage shield (Priest)
Lattice Strike – Melee attack enhanced by damage shield present on Priest (Priest)
Lattice Wall – Light magic against front row and light retaliation for team until next turn (Priest)
Ostracizing Strike – Melee attack that disenchants and curses a single target (Priest)
Defensive Regeneration – Grant target ally regeneration and enhanced defense (Priest)
Elemental Blessing – Grants ally damage shield and enhanced elemental power. Buff is lost when damage shield is destroyed (Priest)
Elemental Healing – Heal single target and enhance elemental resistance (Priest)

Lattice Reflection – Until the Priest’s next turn, a flat proportion of all damage dealt to his damage shield is reflected as untyped retaliation damage back to the attacker. The shield absorbs the original damage normally. (Priest)
Parallel Restoration – Heal single target and grant it damage shield based on amount healed (Priest)
Pure Blessing – Grants ally damage shield and enhanced affliction resistance. Buff is lost when damage shield is destroyed (Priest)
Strike Blessing – Grants ally damage shield and light damage add. Buff is lost when damage shield is destroyed (Priest)
Surging Blessing – Grants ally damage shield and mana surge. Buff is lost when damage shield is destroyed (Priest)
Extra Protection – Grant ally with full health damage shield (Priest)
Prayer of Protection – Restore damage shield based on divinity. (Priest)
Quickening Damage Shield – Quicken all allies with damage shield (Priest)
Restore Damage Shield – Restores value to damage shield (Priest)
Solid Lattice – Minimize next damage against ally with damage shield (Priest)

Sun Domain – Deals light damage to all enemies on each of the Priest’s turns. Requires a minimum divinity to activate and drains divinity each turn. Generates divinity when the Priest uses light abilities. (Priest)
Basic Vitality – Restores all allies to a given percentage of maximum health (Combat Medic)
Emergency Resurrection – If an ally would die before next turn, it returns to life with one health (Combat Medic)
Final Stand – Grants all endangered allies enduring (Combat Medic)
Planned Remedies – Heal ally with lowest health at beginning of next x turns (Combat Medic)
Reactive Heal, Group – Heals all allies next time an enemy uses an attack that damages all. (Combat Medic)
Renewing Onslaught – Melee attack that cures all on critical (Combat Medic)
Victorious Block – Melee attack that guarantees block on kill (Combat Medic)
Victorious Remedy – Attack and purge on kill (Combat Medic)
Victorious Rescue – Melee attack and heal ally with lowest health on kill (Combat Medic)
Vital Avoidance – Group heal that enhances dodge for all allies until they next take damage (Combat Medic)
Vital Strength – Group heal that enhances damage for all allies until they next take damage (Combat Medic)
Vital Vengeance – Heal target ally, and guarantee counter next time they are attacked (Combat Medic)
Defense Heal – Heal and enhance defense (Combat Medic)
Divine Arsenal – Grants all allies enhanced damage and heal on attack proc based on divinity consumed. Consumes all divinity (Combat Medic)
Grand Reknitting – Grants all allies regeneration until they are damaged (Combat Medic)
Invigorated Strength – Whenever target is healed before next turn, enhance its damage based on heal value (Combat Medic)
Quick Heal 2 – Move action heal, costs mana but is not prepared (Combat Medic)
Reactive Heal, Moderate – Grants moderate heal to next ally dealt damage (Combat Medic)
Vital Inspiration – Heal for single target that grants mana surge until they next take damage (Combat Medic)
Vital Speed – Heal for single target with lowest health that grants enhanced speed until they next take damage (Combat Medic)
Perilous Divinity – Grants one endangered ally increased healing received. Generates divinity. (Combat Medic)
Prayer for Rescue – Increases cast speed of heals. At high levels, grants a chance for heals to refund mana (Combat Medic)
Reactive Heal, Minor – Grants low level heal to next ally dealt damage (Combat Medic)
Vital Regeneration – Prepared heal for single target that grants regeneration until the next time they take damage (Combat Medic)

War Domain – War Domain: Increases the damage of all allies each turn. Requires a minimum divinity to activate and drains divinity each turn. Generates divinity when any ally scores a critical hit while the domain is active. (Combat Medic)
Banish Spirits – Cull all intangible enemies (Exorcist)
Channeled Light – Channeled light magic against single (Exorcist)
Disenchanting Light – Light magic attack versus all with chance to disenchant. More powerful against fewer enemies (Exorcist)
Divine Force – Light damage versus all and delay based on divinity used (Exorcist)
Divine Storm – Random light magic attacks based on divinity (Exorcist)
Exorcism Rite – High damage single target light magic attack against intangible (Exorcist)
Exorcism Service – High damage light damage versus all intangible (Exorcist)
Fatal Exorcism – Kill target intangible enemy (Exorcist)
Imprisoning Exorcism – Incapacitate all intangible enemies (Exorcist)
Mana Exorcism – Magic light attack with ghost touch that damages mana (Exorcist)
Manifest Spirit – Light damage and disenchant intangible from intangible (Exorcist)
Searing Light – Light magic attack versus single that causes field-based light bleed (Exorcist)
Bring to the Light – Afflict all intangible enemies with light exposure (Exorcist)
Death Ward, Lasting – Target cannot be affected by death effects for a period (Exorcist)
Fire Healing – Heal an ally and grant it a fire add to its next attack (Exorcist)
Ghost Hunter – Grant target ally period light damage add and ghost touch (Exorcist)
Sanctify Blood – “Let the light of Hugh protect your blood.” – Ally cannot be affected by life drains until Exorcist’s next turn (Exorcist)
Spectral Arsenal – Grants ghost touch to all ally attacks (Exorcist)
Turn to Spirit – Target enemy becomes intangible for a period, weaken enemy damage (Exorcist)
Divine Shelter – Prevent the next affliction from affecting target. Consumes one divinity (Exorcist)

Exorcism Domain – Exorcism Domain: Drains mana from all enemies on each of the Exorcist’s turns. Requires a minimum divinity to activate and drains divinity each turn. Generates divinity based on total mana lost or spent by all enemies while the domain is active. (Exorcist)
Ghost Prayer – Attacks of allies gain ghost touch. At high levels, attacks also have increased critical chance versus intangible enemies (Exorcist)
Possession Guard – Prevents target from being possessed until exorcist’s next turn. Generates divinity (Exorcist)
Protection from the Dark – Enhance dark resistance of all allies (Exorcist)
Spirit Pause – Delay an intangible enemy (Exorcist)
Arise and Strike – Target incapacitated ally loses incapacitated and makes a powerful melee attack against random enemy (Preacher)
Blessing Slam – Enchant Preacher with light empowerment then make melee attack. Grant light empowerment to team on proc (Preacher)
Brilliant Nightmare – Insidious light magic damage against single incapacitated enemy (Preacher)
Divine Sleep – Incapacitate all enemies based on total divinity and consume all divinity (Preacher)
Hallowed Ground – Creates light damage aura based on divinity (Preacher)
Holy Nightmare – High light illusory damage versus all incapacitated enemies (Preacher)
Holy Visions – Light magic damage versus all incapacitated enemies (Preacher)
Just Sleep – Incapacitate against single enemy enhanced by justice (Preacher)
Light of Sleep – Prepared magic light attack that causes incapacitate (Preacher)

Rest Domain – Rest Domain: Delays all enemies on each of the Preacher’s turns. Requires a minimum divinity to activate and drains divinity each turn. Generates divinity each tick while any ally or the Preacher himself is incapacitated. (Preacher)
Blast Ascension – Deals light melee damage to all enemies. Costs mana and requires full divinity (Zealot)

Inspire Fervor – Attack target. Quicken all allies. Any ally over 1000 timer makes free attack versus target (Zealot)

A Warcry-powered melee fighter who grows stronger as the battlefield fills with enemies and emptier as it fills with graves. Her Warcries scale with total enemy rank, her challenge relationship escalates through three states of control, and every fallen ally sharpens her next strike through ancestral fury.

A companion-sacrificing death mage who converts her companion's life into field-wide corruption and damage. She raises allies into corruption, layers Eros and Thanatos into her trap and buff toolkit, and keeps herself alive by ensuring her companion absorbs the killing blow in her place.

A fragility specialist who systematically dismantles enemy defenses. She builds fragile value through ranged attacks, traps, and companion abilities, exploits it with guaranteed criticals and heartstrike, and creates a compounding loop where every critical hit makes the target progressively more vulnerable.

A scroll-cycling arcanist who fights through predetermined sequences of elemental, control, and protective magic. Each scroll advances one step per use toward a final payoff, multiple scrolls can run simultaneously, and completing any scroll rewards her with mana and a damage spike.

A nature-themed support caster who turns regeneration into a delivery system for powerful secondary effects. Each Bloom ability grants an ally regeneration that, when it restores them to full health, triggers a distinct payoff — from field-wide damage to purges to retaliation — while her capstone balances regeneration's vitality efficiency against burst healing.

A charm-and-illusion controller who builds a pipeline from illusory damage through charm into possession. She maintains influence on enemies to amplify possessed attacks, expends focus charges for bonus effects on her most powerful abilities, and passively charms any enemy she deals illusory damage to.

A three-modifier melee specialist who keeps all three offensive tools — clobber, penetrate, and shatter — cycling and cross-amplifying throughout a fight. Her stays-prepared abilities punish enemies for triggering their conditions, Flexible Blows grows more powerful with each consecutive use, and using any one modifier boosts the other two for the following turn.

A dodge-and-pounce duelist who converts every evasion into an offensive opportunity. He chains dodge reactions into melee attacks, builds advantage through flanking and blind exploitation, manages his form position to unlock Leopard-gated tools, and uniquely retains a chance to dodge even critical hits.

A mechanical commander who fights alongside a single powerful Arsenal companion. She summons her Arsenal to provide sustained fire support, then commands it to unleash devastating one-time attacks, protects it from damage by absorbing hits herself, and generates expertise through their coordinated actions.

A self-stripping dark caster who grows more powerful the less he has. He deliberately loses his own enchantments to fuel mana and magic power stacks, disenchants enemies before punishing them, and weaponizes the forsaken condition as both a cost and a tool.

A sleep-exploitation specialist who turns incapacitated enemies into prey. She builds a field of sleeping targets, drains their life and mana, possesses them en masse, and remains dangerous even when put to sleep herself through her Somnambulism capstone.

A brand-and-trap arcanist who layers two distinct families of persistent effects. Brands sit on enemies as elemental hexes waiting to activate, traps lie in wait on the field, and when an enemy triggers a trap it detonates every hex on itself simultaneously through Cascade of Ruin.

A heavy-throwing bruiser who specializes in punishing large, high-health enemies. She scales her Goliath abilities off enemy maximum health, chains decimation through ricochets and cleaves, and transfers melee modifiers onto ranged attacks to make every throw hit as hard as a swing.

A sword-drawing duelist who cycles between sheathed and drawn states to access increasingly powerful initial strikes. Her first action of each wave unlocks the full Iaijutsu suite, Sheathing Attack and Iaijutsu Slash return her to the sheathed state mid-fight, and the capstone gives her a chance to automatically re-sheathe after every attack.

A freedom fighter who thrives under pressure. He purges control and movement afflictions from allies while quickening them, scales his justice and distress tools with how outnumbered the party is, and fights best when the odds are stacked against him — which is exactly when his capstone kicks in hardest.

An elemental wish-caster who channels her companion's element into team-wide buffs at the cost of that companion's momentum. She draws on djinn and elemental companions to shape retaliation, damage adds, and attunements for the whole party, and grows more powerful in their associated element the longer they fight together.

Named for the first master of lightning, the Blitzknecht school occupies one corner of the Abyssal Lands with the particular pride of an institution that considers itself the fastest and most aggressive of the four academies. Their collaboration with the Abyssals was enthusiastic rather than reluctant, and their graduates filled officer roles in the Abyssal armies with a comfort that has made postwar reconciliation difficult. The school still operates, because the alternative was a siege nobody wanted, and the instructors teach the same curriculum they always have.

The fire school produces practitioners whose combat philosophy matches their element — overwhelming, consuming, difficult to redirect once committed. Feuerknecht graduates were among the most visible Abyssal collaborators during the war, their destructive capabilities deployed against Concord forces in engagements that veterans remember specifically and bitterly. The school's current leadership maintains that the collaboration was a matter of survival rather than ideology. Most people who fought against Feuerknecht graduates find this distinction less meaningful than the school does.

Earth magic lends itself to endurance and fortification, and the Drecknecht school produced some of the most effective defensive practitioners the Abyssal forces deployed. Where Blitzknecht and Feuerknecht graduates led assaults, Drecknecht alumni held positions — the unglamorous, grinding work of keeping ground taken. Five years later they are perhaps the least visible of the four schools' graduates, their defensive specialty translating more quietly into postwar life than their more aggressive counterparts.

The water school carries the same collaboration history as its three counterparts, though its elemental focus lends itself to adaptability and flow rather than the more immediately destructive applications of fire and lightning. Trinknecht graduates tend to be the most politically flexible of the four schools' alumni, a quality that served them during the war and continues to serve them in the complicated postwar landscape, where the ability to move with circumstances rather than against them has genuine survival value.

Some Spellsword graduates were never particularly loyal to their schools' elemental traditions, and even less loyal to the Abyssal cause their academies endorsed. Mercenaries took their training and sold it to whoever would pay, serving Concord forces as readily as Abyssal ones during the war and paying no particular price for it afterward. They carry the most comfortable postwar reputation of any Spellsword tradition, which the academy loyalists resent considerably.

Where most Spellswords treat arcane magic as a complement to their blade work, the Force Weaver inverted that relationship, building their combat style on magical force as the foundation with the sword playing a supporting role. The tradition developed outside the four schools' framework, drawing on general Spellsword training redirected toward a more overtly magical application. Force Weavers exist at the edge of what distinguishes a Spellsword from a combat wizard, and practitioners on both sides of that line have opinions about which side of it the Force Weaver actually occupies.

The insight that drove the Transmuter tradition was simple and radical — that the enchantment work Spellswords applied to their weapons could also be applied to themselves. Transmuters augment their own physical capabilities alongside their blade and magic work, producing a fighting style that is harder to categorize and harder to predict than standard Spellsword practice. The tradition developed independently of the four schools, and its practitioners tend to have a flexible relationship with the collaboration history that most Spellswords carry.

The academies reserved their best graduates for Myrmidon training, producing elite protectors for Abyssal dignitaries and high-ranking commanders. They were, by any measure, excellent at their work. Five years after the war's end, that excellence is precisely the problem — the Concord nations are aware that somewhere in the Abyssal Lands there are highly trained, deeply loyal practitioners whose charges are either dead, imprisoned, or in hiding, and who have not necessarily transferred that loyalty anywhere safer.

A quiet rejection of the Spellsword orthodoxy, the Nightblade tradition challenges the fundamental assumption that one foe deserves absolute focus. Where the standard Spellsword philosophy builds entirely around the Challenge — the singular obsession with a chosen enemy — the Nightblade sees wisdom in adaptability, moving between opponents, accepting damage as part of a rhythm rather than a failure of commitment. Their elemental focus on dark as void rather than darkness proper reflects the same philosophy: not the presence of something malevolent, but the deliberate absence of limitation.

The pinnacle of Spellsword mastery carries a theological dimension that the elemental schools, with their founder-worship and collaborative history, never quite achieved. Sword Saints have moved through multiple elemental traditions toward light as synthesis — not a fifth element so much as the convergence of all four, a clarity achieved through comprehensive mastery rather than singular focus. Their strikes carry the certainty of practitioners who have stopped fighting to prove something and started fighting to finish something. Elia Scarlotto, trained outside the system by a master the academies killed, pursuing her revenge through every elemental tradition he taught her, is perhaps following a path toward this without having chosen it.

The Arachnians are gone and their devices don't manufacture themselves, which means someone has to find them. Scavengers operate mostly within Valisian waters, diving shipwrecks and picking through coastal ruins for artifacts that predate every current civilization. They work outside the crew structure that defines most Valisian life, tolerated rather than integrated, valued for what they bring up from the deep rather than for any loyalty to a particular flag. What they find they sell, keep, or quietly deliver to whichever Order has made them the better offer.

The Alchemist's work happens before the battle rather than during it — potions, compounds, and potables prepared carefully in advance and deployed when the moment requires. The tradition exists entirely independent of Teknos devices, practiced by chemists and herbalists across all three Concord nations, but a Teknixian Alchemist brings the device's capabilities to bear on both preparation and application, producing effects that purely mundane alchemy cannot replicate. Calpurnia Moss has a particular appreciation for preparation, having learned through long experience that improvisation is what happens when preparation fails.

Where most Teknixian work produces immediate effects, the Artificer's creations improve over time — devices that learn, adapt, and become more capable the longer they are in use. There is something of the Arachnian philosophy in this approach, a sympathy for technology that develops rather than simply functions. Artificers tend toward patience as a personality trait, which is either cause or effect of working in a tradition where the best results require years rather than minutes.

The Engineer's relationship with Teknos technology is the most practically minded of any subclass — construction, fortification, siege equipment, the unglamorous infrastructure of warfare and peacetime alike. Machinists build weapons of war, but Engineers build everything else, including the machines that move those weapons into position. During the Abyssal war they were invaluable on both sides, their skills too useful for either faction to refuse, which has left them with the most politically complicated postwar reputation of the purely practical Teknixian traditions.

Every device breaks, degrades, or proves poorly suited to the specific situation it encounters. The Tinker exists to fix that — modifying, repairing, and adapting Teknos devices and mundane technology alike to better serve whatever purpose is currently required. The tradition values improvisation over precision, a willingness to work with what's available rather than what's ideal. Tinkers are often found in the Abyssal Lands, where ideal is rarely on offer and functional is the best anyone can hope for.

Explosive applications of Teknos technology serve military and civilian purposes with equal enthusiasm, which is either reassuring or concerning depending on one's perspective. Bombers found consistent employment during the Abyssal war, and the same skills translate cleanly to mining, demolition, and the occasional very emphatic resolution of a dispute. The Corrupted Order has produced Bombers whose applications lean exclusively toward the destructive end of the spectrum, using crude facsimile devices that the Ancient and New Orders regard with the specific horror of people watching their tradition desecrated.

The Teknos device's capacity to function as a ranged weapon has been developed most deliberately by the Gunslinger tradition, which approaches accuracy and technique with something approaching the Archer's professional rigor. Called shots, precise targeting, the discipline of knowing exactly where something will hit before it hits — these are Gunslinger concerns, and the tradition has more in common with Samson Graves' Hunter's Guild background than either would necessarily want to admit.

The most innovative of the Teknixian traditions, the Savant pursues self-fueling device designs that operate beyond the standard limitations of Teknos technology — creations that generate their own resources rather than consuming finite ones. Whether this represents a genuine understanding of how the Arachnians intended their devices to eventually develop, or an inspired accident of experimentation, is a question the Savant tradition debates with considerable enthusiasm and no consensus.

Catapults, arbalests, siege engines, the heavy machinery of organized warfare — the Machinist builds what armies need to take and hold ground. The tradition exists entirely independently of Teknos devices in its mundane form, practiced by military engineers across all three Concord nations, but a Teknixian Machinist produces equipment that operates at a different level of capability entirely. During the Abyssal war, Machinists on both sides were responsible for some of the conflict's most devastating engagements, a legacy that sits heavily in a world still rebuilding.

The pinnacle of Teknixian practice is not defined by what a practitioner can build or destroy but by what they understand. The Reliquarian has developed a genuine comprehension of Arachnian technology at a foundational level — not just how to use the devices but why they work, what the Arachnians intended, and what the symbiotic relationship between device and practitioner was truly meant to become. In a world where the creators are gone, betrayed by the race they mentored and erased from history, the Reliquarian carries something irreplaceable: the closest thing remaining to the Arachnians' actual knowledge, preserved in the relationship between a living person and a device that is, in its own way, still alive.

A ranged specialist who embraces blindness as a permanent condition rather than a handicap. She self-blinds to unlock more powerful attacks, spreads blind to enemies to set up exploitation, and never truly wastes a shot — every miss becomes a second chance against a random enemy.

A holy warrior who maintains a network of ongoing enchantments across the party. Sigils reserve mana but persist indefinitely and transfer freely between allies, the Chaplain generates divinity through blocking rather than spellcasting, and Lingering Sigil ensures no ally loses their protection the instant it's reassigned.

A spectral mounted warrior who turns glancing blows into momentum. He rides a ghost steed into intangibility, harvests spirit power from near-misses and blocked hits, and converts every glancing blow against himself or his mount into immediate speed for the next charge.

A shadow-dwelling rogue who grows more dangerous the longer she stays hidden. Her Dusk abilities scale with accumulated hidden duration, the Gathering Dusk capstone compounds that value across multiple hidden periods, and her trap and rune toolkit lets her threaten the field without ever emerging from the dark.

A corruption-spreading technomancer who chains afflictions across the entire enemy field. Persistent abilities relay damage, possession, and misfortune from enemy to enemy in sequence, detonations amplify curses and malediction, and the Forking Jump capstone turns every chain into a potential branching cascade.

A companion-bonded fire mage whose power peaks precisely when her companion dies. She sacrifices it deliberately for damage, draws mana and fire power from its death through the Payback family, and with Entwined in Death her own mortality and her companion's become fully interchangeable triggers.

A martial artist who gates elemental fist abilities behind elemental spellcasting. Using a fire spell readies Fire Punch, using a water spell readies Water Punch, and Rotating Fist lets her cycle through either fist sequence without costs or prerequisites — rewarding the player who alternates spell and strike in practiced sequence.

A berserking bard who channels fury into healing rather than just destruction. She spreads berserk to allies to amplify their damage, then uses that same berserk state as a catalyst for stronger heals and purges, with Raging Mercy stacking those bonuses when she's berserk and healing a berserk ally simultaneously.
